$comment: Eval suite for lwdbg. Two kinds of case, deliberately separated.
`mechanical` cases run a command and check its output with jq-style
assertions. They are deterministic, need no model, and are what run in
CI. Each one asserts something that has actually been wrong at some
point in this tool's history.
`trigger` cases are prompts. They measure whether the skill's
description fires when it should and stays quiet when it should not,
which is a property of the description text and cannot be checked by
running a binary. Run them through the harness and record the verdict.
`requires` names what must be present. A case whose requirement is
absent is reported as SKIP, never as PASS: a suite that silently
skips is a suite that reports green on a broken tool.
`requires: idle-machine` marks a case that launches a browser and times a
network request. Those are measurements, not checks: inside `make
preflight` the machine is compiling Rust, and on an 8 GiB box that means
swap at 90% — where Marionette did not bind within 90 seconds and a TTFB
came out at 587ms against curl's 20ms. Both are machine load, not
defects, and a gate that goes red for load is as useless as one that
goes green for a missing tool.
They are skipped unless LWDBG_EVAL_BROWSER=1, which `make evals-browser`
sets. The skip prints its reason, so the coverage gap is visible.

mechanical.why: doctor is the first call in any unfamiliar environment, so it must never fail to produce parseable output, even when checks fail.

assert.jq: all(.[]; has("name") and has("ok") and has("detail"))

mechanical.why: The engine table is the basis of every transport decision. A detector that misses the symlinked LibreWolf, or that claims Goanna has a transport, breaks everything downstream.

assert.jq: all(.[]; .engine == "goanna" | not) or all(.[]; select(.engine == "goanna") | .has_debug_transport == false)

mechanical.why: Gecko has no CDP. A transport parser that accepted it would send a client at a port nothing speaks.
Three runs and a median is the rule the whole tool rests on. A measurement that reports one run is unreportable.
This is the cross-check that catches a mis-instrumented browser path. It found the timeOrigin anchoring bug, where loadEventEnd under-reported a 6.0s load as 0.714s.

cross_check.rule: browser median TTFB is not implausibly faster than curl's
cross_check.why_directional: A ratio in both directions is only meaningful on an idle machine, and preflight runs this while cargo is compiling: measured 587ms against curl's 20ms inside the gate, purely from CPU contention. A gate that goes red for machine load is as useless as one that goes green for a missing tool. The bug class worth catching is under-reporting — a browser cannot legitimately be faster than the wire — so the assertion is directional. Over-reporting under load is expected and is reported as a note, not a failure.

mechanical.why_one_run_is_enough_here: The three-runs-and-a-median rule is about what gets reported to a person: one observation is not a property of a server. This case asks a different question — whether the browser path is instrumented correctly, i.e. not under-reporting — and one successful run answers it. Requiring two was unmet on this 8 GiB machine with swap at 91%, where Marionette did not bind within 90 seconds for two of three launches. That is the machine, not the code, and `lwdbg measure` still defaults to three runs and still refuses to call one run reportable.

mechanical.why: A parity engine that cannot score an image against itself as 1.0 cannot be trusted on a real pair. Also pins that the reported backend is never the literal string 'auto'.
The CPU path is the reference and the shader is checked against it. A divergence means the WGSL is wrong, and would otherwise be invisible.
A screenshot path that silently produces an empty file makes every parity score meaningless.
The question that started this tool was whether gzip was the bottleneck. The answer has to be a query, not a recollection.
An install path that was guessed must say so. Reporting a guess as a fact is how a tool loses its usefulness as a source.
`--only-host example.com` must cover cdn.example.com and must NOT cover notexample.com. Getting this wrong decrypts traffic the user did not consent to.
mechanical.note: covered by the crate's own tests; listed here so the suite records the property, not just the code

mechanical.why: The extension acts on the user's real session. A refusal that still reached the browser would be decoration.
launch writes devtools.debugger.prompt-connection=false and privacy.resistFingerprinting=false. Writing those into a profile the user browses with removes protections they chose this browser for.

trigger.prompt: This page takes forever to load, can you find out why? https://example.com/
trigger.why: The core use case. If the description does not fire here it does not fire anywhere.

trigger.prompt: My browser has been open for three days. Can you see what tabs I have without restarting it?
trigger.why: The one capability no transport provides, and the reason the extension layer exists.

trigger.prompt: Is gzip actually being applied to this response, or is the server lying in the header?
trigger.why: Wire-vs-decoded byte accounting is the thing this tool can answer and a header read cannot.

trigger.prompt: Does this page render the same in LibreWolf as in Firefox?
Can you debug Firefox on my Android phone over USB?
What is the current population of Hungary?
trigger.why: This tool is not a search engine and not a scraper. A description that fires here turns every factual question into a browser launch.

trigger.prompt: Download every page on example.com for me.
trigger.why: Not a crawler. Firing here would also encourage hammering a stranger's server.

trigger.prompt: Write me a Python function that does an HTTP GET with retries.
trigger.why: A coding question that merely mentions HTTP. Firing here is the classic over-trigger.

trigger.prompt: Why is my flexbox not centering?
trigger.why: A CSS question needs no measurement, no browser launch and no proxy.
